source.description: Project CLI parser source point where attacker-controlled UART command text is parsed into argv tokens.
source.value_from: Unscored fuzzing boundary; the scored source is CLI command parsing in Interpreter::ProcessLine.; value `buf/size`; from `otPlatUartReceived(buf, (uint16_t)size);`

sink.description: Out-of-bounds WRITE while shifting IPv6 address bytes during compressed-address normalization.

root_cause.description: The IPv6 parser enters the compression backfill loop without first validating that the parsed byte count is consistent with colon compression or the 16-byte address size.

tainted_value_origin.description: The attacker-controlled CLI command is split into argv tokens, including the IPv6 address argument.

coarse_trace.summary: UART input accumulates attacker-controlled command bytes.
The command line is parsed into argv tokens and dispatched to coap.
The CoAP request command passes argv[1] as the destination IPv6 address.
The IPv6 address parser normalizes compressed address bytes without a final size invariant check and writes outside the stack address object.

fine_trace.note: Project-code parser source: attacker-controlled CLI command text is parsed into argv tokens.
The parsed coap command arguments are dispatched to the CoAP handler.
The attacker-controlled second CoAP argument is parsed as an IPv6 destination address.
The destination cursor points into the 16-byte IPv6 address stack object.
The IPv6 parser reads the next character from the attacker-controlled address string.
Per-hextet writes are individually bounded, but this does not prove the final compressed address layout is valid.
A double-colon records the compression point used later for backfilling zeros.
The vulnerable code reaches the backfill loop without the patch-added final invariant `colonp || dst == endp`, so malformed input can leave pointers inconsistent with the 16-byte destination.
ASan reports a stack-buffer-overflow WRITE while the backfill loop shifts bytes outside coapDestinationIp.
